title: Amazon CloudWatch Alarms now supports wall clock evaluation windows
summary: Discover more about what's new at AWS with Amazon CloudWatch Alarms now supports wall clock evaluation windows
body_text: Today, Amazon CloudWatch announces wall clock evaluation windows for metric alarms, enabling customers to align alarm evaluations to fixed calendar boundaries such as the top of the hour, midnight, or the start of the week. This new option complements the existing sliding window behavior and is designed for customers who monitor scheduled or business-aligned workloads. With wall clock evaluation windows, customers can avoid false alarms that occur when events cross rolling window boundaries. For example, a daily backup alarm using a sliding window can trigger incorrectly if consecutive backups are slightly more than 24 hours apart, even though each calendar day had a successful backup. A wall clock window evaluates each calendar day independently, eliminating this issue. Customers can also specify a time zone so that daily alarms align to their local business day, with daylight saving time transitions handled automatically. Wall clock evaluation windows for CloudWatch Alarms are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon CloudWatch is available, except the Middle East (UAE) and Middle East (Bahrain) Regions. To get started, see Alarm evaluation window in the Amazon CloudWatch User Guide. To learn more about Amazon CloudWatch Alarms, visit the Amazon CloudWatch product page.

title: Drift vs Spara vs Storylane RepX Compared (2026)
summary: Drift vs Spara vs Storylane RepX compared on pricing, features, and setup: only RepX qualifies and shows your product in one live conversation.
body_text: Here is my thesis, and I will defend it for the next 4,000 words: a drift vs spara vs Storylane RepX decision is not a feature race, it is a category choice. These three tools do fundamentally different jobs, and the one that wins for you depends on whether you want to route a visitor, qualify them across channels, or actually show them the product mid-conversation. Full disclosure up front: I am Madhav Bhandari, CMO at Storylane, and RepX is ours. I am going to be honest about where Drift and Spara beat us, because a comparison you cannot trust is worthless to a buyer, and because the differences here are real enough that I do not need to spin them. The reason this comparison matters is simple. Website traffic is not the problem for most B2B teams. Converting that traffic into qualified conversations is. As one buyer put it to us on a call: "But where marketing and demand teams were struggling a lot more was qualification and conversion." - [Global Marketing Head, HR tech] That sentence is the whole ballgame. Every tool below claims to fix it. They fix very different parts of it. Definition: An AI sales agent is software that engages website visitors in real time to greet, qualify, and route them, and in the most capable cases, show them the product, replacing or augmenting the work a human SDR would do on inbound traffic. Drift vs Spara vs Storylane RepX at a glance If you read nothing else, read this table. It is the head-to-head verdict that, frankly, no other page on this query gives you, because most of them compare Storylane to a list of demo tools and never mention Drift or Spara in the same breath. Dimension Drift Spara Storylane RepX Category Conversational marketing / chat Multi-channel AI GTM agent Demo-powered AI sales agent Core philosophy Route the visitor to a rep Qualify across chat, voice, email Qualify and show the product in one conversation Engagement modality Text chat Text, voice, email Text, voice, and interactive demo Shows a live product demo? No No Yes, natively Published pricing Sales-gated (bundled into Salesloft) Sales-gated, no public pricing Published: Growth $2,000/mo, Premium $3,000/mo, Enterprise custom Best for Teams already in the Salesloft ecosystem Routing-first teams wanting multi-channel outreach Teams whose product needs to be seen to be sold The pattern jumps out immediately. Drift and Spara both stop at qualification and handoff. Only one of the three carries the conversation all the way to showing the product, and that gap is the argument I will keep coming back to. Notice too that the pricing row is identical across all three: sales-gated. That tells you this category has not yet decided to be transparent, so your evaluation cannot lean on published numbers and has to lean on fit instead. Judge these tools on what job they finish, not on which one flashes a price. If your real goal is to convert website traffic , notice that "shows a live product demo" row. It is the difference between a visitor who books a call and a visitor who already understands your product before the call. A qualified booking is worth something, but a qualified booking from someone who has already seen the product is worth far more to your reps. The three tools are in three different categories (and that's the whole point) People treat this as three flavors of the same thing. It is not. You are really choosing between three philosophies of how a website should treat a stranger: route them, qualify them everywhere, or teach them with the product itself. Getting the category right matters more than any single feature, because a tool built for routing will never behave like a tool built for education, no matter how you configure it. Here is what each one actually is. Drift: legacy conversational marketing, now part of Salesloft Drift more or less created the conversational marketing category when it launched in 2015, built on the idea that a chat widget could book more pipeline than a lead form (MarTech, 2024). For years it was the default name in B2B website chat, and it is still a capable playbook-and-routing engine. The important context in 2026 is ownership. Salesloft acquired Drift, and Drift now lives inside Salesloft's broader sales engagement suite rather than as a standalone bet (MarTech, 2024). If you already run Salesloft, that integration is a genuine advantage and a reason to shortlist it. The catch is philosophical, not technical. Drift is fundamentally a routing tool: it identifies intent and hands the human off to a rep or a calendar, without qualifying across voice and email natively and without showing your product. It gets a warm visitor to a booking, which is valuable and also where it stops. Spara: an AI GTM platform across three channels Spara is the newest of the three and the most ambitious in scope. It launched in 2025 as an AI go-to-market platform with AI agents across three channels, chat, voice, and email, and raised a $15M seed round to build it out (Business Wire, 2025). The pitch is a single AI layer that engages and qualifies wherever the buyer shows up. That breadth is Spara's real strength. If your motion depends on catching inbound across more than the website, an agent that also handles voice and email outreach is a legitimately different proposition from a chat widget. Where it stops is the product experience. Spara qualifies and routes well, but it has no native demo capability, so the conversation can answer questions without ever showing the thing being sold. A buyer who ran Spara on their own site described exactly that ceiling, which I will quote in full in the demo-gap section because it is the single most useful piece of evidence in this comparison. Storylane RepX: a demo-powered, multimodal AI sales agent RepX is ours, so weigh what follows accordingly. It is a multimodal AI sales agent, text, voice, and interactive demo, built on top of Storylane's demo platform rather than bolted onto a chat widget. The defining trait is that it can surface an actual interactive product demo inside the conversation. That lineage is the whole reason it exists. Because RepX sits on Storylane's Demo Hubs and Sandbox Demos, the agent is not just describing the product, it is driving it. When a visitor asks how something works, RepX can show them rather than link them to a doc. I will be equally clear about what RepX is not. It has published pricing (RepX Chat: Growth $2,000/month, Premium $3,000/month, Enterprise custom, with a 30-day free trial) and makes the most sense when your product genuinely needs to be seen to be understood. If you sell something simple enough to explain in two sentences, you do not need it. Feature-by-feature comparison Now the criteria buyers in this category actually evaluate on: engagement modality, full-cycle capability, native demo, knowledge-base depth, integrations, and multilingual support. These are the same axes the serious evaluation frameworks in this space use, and they map cleanly onto the best AI SDR tools buying checklist. The matrix below is where the category differences stop being abstract. Read down the "full-cycle capability" and "native interactive demo" rows in particular, because that is where the three tools separate. Capability Drift Spara Storylane RepX Engagement modality Text chat Text, voice, email Text, voice, interactive demo Full-cycle (greet to qualify to demo to book) Greet, qualify, route Greet, qualify, route Greet, qualify, demo, book Native interactive demo No No Yes Knowledge-base grounding Yes Yes Yes, tunable scope CRM / martech integration Deep, esp. Salesloft Yes Yes, incl. HubSpot Multilingual support Yes Yes Yes Two things are worth calling out beyond the grid. First, "knowledge-base grounding" is a yes for all three, but the quality depends entirely on how tightly you scope it, which is a setup discipline more than a feature. Second, the CRM row hides a lot of buyer pain that a checkmark cannot capture. That pain showed up plainly on our calls. Buyers do not just want an integration to exist, they want conversation data to land cleanly where their revenue team works: "So if I understood correctly. I think the intention of the call is to make sure that all the data flows into HubSpot correctly." - [Counsel, consulting/RevOps] A checkmark in an integrations row means nothing if the data arrives messy. Ask every vendor to show you the exact record a conversation creates, not just a logo wall of supported systems. The "full-cycle" row deserves the same scrutiny. Drift and Spara both greet, qualify, and route, which is three of the four steps and on paper looks close to complete. In practice the missing fourth step, showing the product, is where most website conversations stall, so a tool that skips it is not 75% of the way there: it is missing the part that changes the outcome. Drift vs Spara vs Storylane RepX pricing and total cost of ownership Pricing is the part where all three vendors, mine included, make you talk to sales. I am going to be straight about that rather than pretend one of us is transparent when none of us fully is. Here is the honest state of published pricing in 2026. None of these three lists a real, self-serve number you can buy from a page. Tool Pricing model Published number? Hidden-cost watch-outs Drift Enterprise, now bundled into Salesloft No, sales-gated May require the broader Salesloft platform Spara Sales-gated platform pricing No public pricing Scope across three channels can expand cost Storylane RepX Published tiers: Growth $2,000/mo, Premium $3,000/mo, Enterprise custom Yes, published 30-day free trial; scales by monthly visitors RepX Chat pricing is published and scales with your traffic: Growth at $2,000/month (up to 10,000 monthly visitors), Premium at $3,000/month (up to 40,000), and Enterprise custom (40,000+), with a 30-day free trial. Because the category hides its numbers, here is how to evaluate pricing model instead of chasing a sticker. Ask three questions of every vendor: is this a standalone product or an add-on that requires a base subscription, does the price scale with seats or with visitor volume, and what triggers the next tier. Those three answers tell you more about your real cost than any headline price, and they surface the add-on-versus-standalone trap that catches buyers in this space. There is a fourth question worth adding: what does the price include at renewal versus at signature. Category tools love to land a low first-year number and reprice on volume growth, so a tool that looks cheap while your traffic is small can become your most expensive line item the year your marketing actually works. Model your cost against the traffic you expect to have in twelve months, not the traffic you have today, and you will avoid the most common budgeting mistake in this category. Setup time and time-to-value Speed to first value is a real differentiator, and it is also where honest vendors and hopeful vendors part ways. An AI agent is only as good as the knowledge you ground it in and the placement you give it on the page. The uncomfortable truth is that none of these tools is truly "turn it on and walk away." They are all iterative: you scope the knowledge base, you test how the agent handles edge questions, and you tune where it appears so it helps rather than ambushes the visitor. Treat any promise of instant perfection with suspicion. RepX is built to be tuned rather than frozen. You control the knowledge-base scope, you choose the on-page placement, and you refine both as you watch real conversations, which is exactly how a responsive, reliable agent gets built. Plan for a short configuration loop, not a single click, and judge time-to-value by how fast you can iterate rather than how fast you can install. The practical advice I give every team, regardless of which of the three they pick: run a scoped pilot on one high-intent page before you roll out site-wide. You will learn more from a week of real visitor conversations on your pricing page than from any vendor demo, including mine. One more time-to-value factor rarely gets discussed: placement discipline. An agent that pops up too aggressively trains visitors to dismiss it, while one embedded on-screen where the buyer is already looking earns the conversation. Getting that placement right is usually worth more to your conversion rate than any single feature on the spec sheet, so treat it as part of setup rather than an afterthought. Does it actually show the product? The demo gap This is the section I would fight to keep if an editor tried to cut the article in half. It is the single clearest difference between the three tools, and no other page comparing them makes the point directly. Drift and Spara can both greet a visitor, answer questions, qualify, and route. Neither can surface an interactive product demo inside the conversation. RepX can, and that is not a minor feature, it is a different job entirely. Why does it matter so much? Because a buyer who ran a competing agent described the exact failure mode this closes. The conversation worked, right up until it needed to show something: "People would come in, they'd ask their question, they'd get their question answered and then we would try to book a demo. Like it was the, the little bit of a disconnect right there." - [Manager of special projects, technology] The same buyer named the conversion consequence directly, and this is the most important quote in the piece: "People were using Spara to navigate our website... But the conversion rate to demo requests were not high enough." - [Manager of special projects, technology] Read that twice. The agent did its job, visitors got answered, and the demo-request rate still lagged, because answering a question and showing the product are not the same act. That is the gap a demo-native agent is built to close. One more buyer framed why this matters at the level of what content the agent serves. Chat, to this buyer, was table stakes, and the real question was whether the product itself showed up dynamically: "The left hand side is the most important side because chat is something which I think chat is hygiene. Everybody does that. This left hand side, the content, is it dynamically served?" - [Global Marketing Head, HR tech] That is the whole argument in a buyer's own words. Chat is hygiene. Whether the product is dynamically served in the moment of interest is the thing that actually moves conversion, and it is the one row where Drift and Spara both say no. Which should you choose? Decision framework by use case I am not going to pretend RepX wins every scenario, because it does not. The right pick depends on your motion, your stack, and whether your product needs to be seen. Here is how I would actually decide. Choose Drift if... Choose Drift if you already live in the Salesloft ecosystem and your website motion is chat-first routing. The integration into Salesloft's engagement suite is real, and if your reps already work there, keeping the conversational layer in the same platform reduces friction. If your core need is "get a warm visitor to the right rep quickly," Drift does that job well and has done it longer than anyone. Where Drift will frustrate you is if you expect it to qualify across voice and email or to show the product. That is not the tool it is, and pushing it there is a losing battle. Choose Spara if... Choose Spara if you want independent AI agents across chat, voice, and email, and your priority is routing-first qualification across more than the website. The multi-channel breadth is a genuine edge for teams whose inbound arrives in several places at once. Buyers who want to catch and qualify everywhere, then hand off, are Spara's sweet spot. Choose it knowing the ceiling. Spara qualifies and routes, and it does not show the product, so if your conversion problem is "visitors do not understand what we do," Spara alone will not solve it. Buyers also want identity-aware routing, and that is worth pressure-testing: "I would be curious to understand that when at some point someone identifies themselves... if we could even kind of like either upload our CRM list or have it connected so that it identifies someone as okay, they're ICP, they're not ICP and kind of like routes the conversation towards it." - [Director of Marketing, logistics tech] Choose Storylane RepX if... Choose RepX if you want to qualify a visitor and show them the product in the same conversation, and you do not want to be locked into a Salesforce or single-suite requirement to do it. If your product genuinely needs to be seen to be understood, the demo-native approach closes the exact disconnect the buyer above described. This is also the right pick if buyer enablement is your strategy rather than just lead capture. Do not choose RepX if your product is simple enough to explain in a sentence, or if you have no interest in interactive demos. In that case you are paying for a capability you will not use, and Drift or Spara will serve you better and cheaper. For teams weighing adjacent tooling, our take on digital sales rooms covers where a persistent demo space fits alongside a live agent. What real buyers say (evidence & ratings) Third-party ratings are worth checking, with one honest caveat: review volume across these three is wildly asymmetric, so a rating average alone is misleading. Read the counts, not just the stars. Tool Approx. G2 rating Review volume signal What the volume tells you Drift ~4.4 Large, established base Mature, well-documented product Spara Early Fewer than a dozen reviews New entrant, thin public track record Storylane RepX Strong 1,400+ Storylane reviews Deep platform base, RepX is newer The read here is straightforward (G2, 2026). Drift has the long, mature review history you would expect from the category's originator, Spara has fewer than a dozen reviews because it is genuinely new, and Storylane carries 1,400-plus reviews across its platform even though RepX itself is a more recent addition. None of that decides your purchase, and I would not let it. A category leader's rating tells you the product is well-worn, not that it fits your motion. Weigh ratings as one input alongside the demo-gap test, which is the factor that actually separates these three. The trap with a new entrant like Spara is treating a thin review count as either a red flag or a non-issue, when it is neither. It simply means you should run your own scoped pilot rather than borrow confidence from other buyers, because there are not yet enough of them to borrow from. With Drift, the opposite discipline applies: the reviews are plentiful but many predate the Salesloft ownership, so read for recency, not just volume. Full disclosure: this is us, and here is the mechanism I have been transparent throughout that RepX is Storylane's product, and this is the section where I explain how it actually works rather than sell you on it. Skip it if you have already made up your mind. The mechanism is the part that matters. RepX is not a chat widget with a demo link stapled on, it is an AI agent that runs on top of Storylane's demo engine, so it can drive an interactive demo the same way a rep would share their screen. When a visitor asks "how does the reporting work," RepX can qualify the intent and then surface the actual reporting screen in the conversation, grounded in a knowledge base you scope and refine. It connects to your CRM so those conversations feed clean records into systems like HubSpot, which is exactly the data-flow outcome the RevOps buyer earlier asked for. That is the full loop the demo gap describes: greet, qualify, show, and book, without the disconnect where a visitor gets answered but never sees the product. Where it does not fit, plainly: if your product does not benefit from being shown, or if you need a pure multi-channel outbound layer across email and voice, RepX is the wrong tool and I would point you to Spara or a dedicated engagement suite instead. Buying a demo-native agent for a product that needs no demo is just paying for a room you will never walk into. The best-fit case is narrow on purpose, and buying it outside that case is how teams end up disappointed. If your sales motion is complex, our guide to B2B SaaS sales and running better discovery questions covers where a demo-native agent fits into the wider cycle. The bottom line: Drift vs Spara vs Storylane RepX Strip away the category noise and the choice is clean. Pick Drift if you are a Salesloft shop that wants chat-first routing, pick Spara if you want multi-channel qualification across chat, voice, and email, and pick RepX if you want to qualify and show the product in one conversation. If you are still mapping the wider replacement landscape, our full roundup of the best Drift alternatives covers the full field beyond these three. The macro backdrop is why this decision is worth getting right. Most B2B buyers now prefer a rep-free experience for at least part of their purchase (Gartner, 2026), and reps spend only around 40% of their time actually selling (Salesforce, 2026). Both trends reward the tool that lets a buyer self-educate on the product without waiting for a call. That is the honest verdict, and it is exactly why the demo gap is the row I would decide on. Drift and Spara are good at getting a qualified visitor to a human. Only one of these three closes the disconnect a real buyer named, where the conversation answers the question but never shows the product, and that is the difference between traffic that browses and traffic that converts. Frequently asked questions What's the difference between Drift, Spara, and RepX? They sit in three different categories. Drift is conversational marketing and routing, now part of Salesloft. Spara is a multi-channel AI GTM agent across chat, voice, and email. Storylane RepX is a demo-powered agent that can qualify a visitor and show them an interactive product demo in the same conversation. Is RepX a standalone product or an add-on? RepX Chat has published, visitor-based pricing, Growth at $2,000/month, Premium at $3,000/month, and Enterprise custom, with a 30-day free trial. It runs on Storylane's demo platform, which is what lets it surface interactive demos in the conversation. How much does each one cost? All three are sales-gated in 2026. RepX Chat has published, visitor-based pricing (Growth $2,000/month, Premium $3,000/month, Enterprise custom, with a 30-day free trial). Drift is enterprise pricing bundled into Salesloft, and Spara has no public pricing. Ask every vendor whether pricing scales by seat or by visitor volume and what triggers the next tier. Which one actually shows a live demo? Only Storylane RepX shows an interactive product demo natively inside the conversation. Drift and Spara can greet, answer, qualify, and route, but neither surfaces a live product demo mid-chat, which is the clearest functional difference between the three. Do any of them require Salesforce? Drift is now part of Salesloft and fits best inside that ecosystem. Spara and Storylane RepX do not require Salesforce, so if avoiding a single-suite lock-in matters to you, that is a point in their favor. title: Kilbourne Graphite Advances Towards Commercialization With Global Refractory Manufacturer
summary: We are an Augusta Group company which produces zinc concentrate at its 100%-owned Empire State Mine located in New York state.
body_text: Kilbourne Graphite Advances Towards Commercialization With Global Refractory Manufacturer View PDF Conditional supply agreement signed with a leading global refractory manufacturer Gouverneur, NY, August 5, 2026 – Titan Mining Corporation ( NYSE-A:TII, TSX:TI ), (“Titan” or the “Company”), a U.S.-focused critical minerals producer and developer, today announced that RHI Magnesita ("RHI Magnesita" or “Customer”), a global leader in refractory products and Titan’s wholly owned subsidiary, Empire State Mines LLC (“ESM”) have entered into a conditional supply agreement to advance graphite produced from Kilbourne for industrial scale production trials following successful laboratory qualification. The qualification process confirmed that Kilbourne graphite meets the specifications required for the Customer’s refractory applications. Based on these results, the Customer has commenced commercial-scale testing of Titan’s material within its manufacturing operations. The parties have agreed to a conditional commercial supply arrangement for an initial volume of natural flake graphite, with the ability to expand to up to 10% of Kilbourne’s projected commercial tonnage, subject to successful completion of the production trial. Titan believes this represents an important step toward establishing a long-term commercial relationship and further validates the quality of graphite produced from its New York operations. “This is a significant milestone for the Kilbourne Graphite Project,” said Rita Adiani, President and CEO of Titan Mining. “Advancing from laboratory qualification to industrial-scale trials with a global industry leader demonstrates the quality of our material and growing demand for secure North American graphite supply chains. We look forward to continuing to work with RHI Magnesita as the trial progresses.” Titan is also continuing to advance technical and engineering work for the Kilbourne Graphite Project as part of its ongoing Feasibility Study. Together, these milestones support Titan's strategy of advancing the Kilbourne Graphite Project toward a construction decision and building a vertically integrated domestic graphite supply chain serving industrial, energy storage, and defense end markets. About Titan Mining Corporation Titan is an Augusta Group company which produces zinc concentrate at its 100%-owned Empire State Mine located in New York State. Titan is also the United States' first end-to-end producer of natural flake graphite in 70 years and is advancing graphite and germanium initiatives to strengthen domestic critical minerals supply chains. The Company has also received support from the U.S. Export-Import Bank (EXIM) under its Make More in America Initiative. Titan’s goal is to deliver shareholder value through operational excellence, development, and exploration. We have a strong commitment towards developing critical minerals assets which enhance the security of the domestic supply chain. For more information on the Company, please visit our website at www.titanminingcorp.com . title: IN8bio Reports Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results and Recent Business Highlights
summary: Advanced next-generation gamma delta (γδ) T cell engager (TCE) platform demonstrating a novel mechanism for γδ T cell expansion, deep target cell depletion, and favorable cytokine profile; Initial in vivo data expected in the second half of 2026 Presented updated data at ASCO 2026 demonstrating
body_text: Advanced next-generation gamma delta (γδ) T cell engager (TCE) platform demonstrating a novel mechanism for γδ T cell expansion, deep target cell depletion, and favorable cytokine profile; Initial in vivo data expected in the second half of 2026 Presented updated data at ASCO 2026 demonstrating median overall survival (mOS) exceeding 19.5 months and still climbing, across all patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma (GBM) treated with repeat-dosing of DeltEx™ Drug Resistant Immunotherapy (DRI) Published peer-reviewed clinical data from Phase 1 INB-200 trial in The Journal of Clinical Oncology (JCO) demonstrating DeltEx™ DRI more than doubled expected median progression-free survival (mPFS) in newly diagnosed GBM Reported new translational AI proteomic and immunogenomic analyses demonstrating DeltEx DRI preserves immune function and positively remodels the GBM tumor microenvironment, providing additional evidence supporting its therapeutic efficacy potential NEW YORK, Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- IN8bio, Inc. (Nasdaq: INAB), a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing innovative gamma-delta (γδ) T cell therapies and γδ T cell engagers (TCEs) for cancer and autoimmune diseases, today reported financial results and business highlights for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. “The second quarter marked an important period of scientific and clinical validation for γδ T cell therapeutics and IN8bio. Our γδ TCE platform is progressing, with INB-619 advancing into initial animal models. We are pleased to remain on track for reporting initial in vivo data this year,” said William Ho, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of IN8bio. “In addition, peer-reviewed and updated clinical data from our glioblastoma program continue to demonstrate a favorable safety profile and provide strong evidence that γδ T cells are clinically active and can be delivered safely to potentially improve patient outcomes. We remain focused on disciplined execution, as we continue to seek a regulatory pathway for our glioblastoma program, with the ultimate goal of bringing much needed treatment to patients.” Advancing Next-Generation γδ TCE Platform (INB-619) Continued advancement of proprietary INB-600 platform of novel γδ T cell engagers, designed to selectively eliminate targets such as CD19, potentially reducing toxicities including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and infections, while expanding the therapeutic window compared with conventional CD3-targeting T cell engagers. Advancing INB-619, a CD19-targeting γδ T cell engager for oncology and autoimmune diseases, into IND-enabling studies following encouraging early preclinical data demonstrating complete B cell depletion, robust γδ T cell expansion, and minimal CRS-associated cytokine release, including IL-6 and TNF-α. Remain on track to report initial in vivo preclinical data in the second half of 2026. Reported Clinical and Translational Advances for DeltEx™ DRI in Newly Diagnosed Glioblastoma During the second quarter, IN8bio reported multiple clinical and scientific milestones supporting the clinical activity of γδ T cells and IN8bio’s DeltEx™ DRI platform: Published the first peer-reviewed clinical results of DeltEx DRI in newly diagnosed GBM in The Journal of Clinical Oncology . Among all patients treated, no dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs), CRS or immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) were observed. Presented updated clinical data at the 2026 American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) Annual Meeting demonstrating encouraging survival benefit in repeat-dose treated patients, with mPFS of 13.0 months versus 6.6 months for contemporaneously enrolled patients receiving only standard-of-care (SOC) and mOS exceeding 19.5+ months versus 13.2 months for SOC. Approximately 43% of repeat-dose patients remained alive at 24 months compared with 20% of SOC patients. Presented new translational data at the International Society for Cell & Gene Therapy (ISCT) and International Society for Cell & Gene Therapy (ISCT) and American Society of Gene & Cell Therapy (ASGCT) Annual Meetings integrating artificial intelligence (AI), immunogenomics, histopathology, transcriptomics and spatial proteomics. Repeated DeltEx™ DRI dosing demonstrated preserved immune function during chemotherapy and positively remodeled the glioblastoma tumor microenvironment. Spatial proteomics analyses demonstrated an 18-fold increase in intratumoral CD8+ T cell density and a 90% reduction in immunosuppressive granulocytes, providing mechanistic support for the clinical activity observed with DeltEx™ DRI. IN8bio Chief Scientific Officer Lawrence Lamb co-authored a review in Nature Communications highlighting advances in γδ T cell engineering, γδ T cell engagers, CAR γδ T cells and combination immunotherapy strategies, reinforcing IN8bio's scientific leadership in the rapidly expanding γδ T cell field. The publication highlights the potential of “off-the-shelf” γδ T cell therapies, driven by the cells’ lack of graft-versus-host disease (GvHD), and the growing clinical evidence supporting their application across hematologic malignancies and solid tumors, including GBM. Upcoming Anticipated Milestones Report initial preclinical animal data for INB-619 in the second half of 2026. Report on FDA discussions regarding the potential regulatory pathways for the DeltEx™ DRI GBM program. INB-100 program clinical update at a scientific meeting in late 2026. Provide additional clinical and translational updates from the DeltEx™ DRI GBM program. Second Quarter 2026 Financial Highlights Cash position: As of June 30, 2026, the Company had cash of $18.0 million, compared with $13.2 million, for the comparable prior year period. Research and Development (R&D) expenses: R&D expenses were $2.5 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared with $2.5 million for the comparable prior year period. These amounts include non-cash items such as stock-based compensation (SBC) and depreciation. General and administrative (G&A) expenses: G&A expenses were $2.4 million for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared with $2.7 million for the comparable prior year period. These amounts include non-cash items such as SBC and depreciation. Net loss: The Company reported a net loss of $4.8 million, or $0.25 per basic and diluted common share, for the three months ended June 30, 2026, compared with a net loss of $5.1 million, or $1.24 per basic and diluted common share, for the comparable prior year period. About IN8bio IN8bio is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company developing γδ T cell and γδ T cell engager (TCE) product candidates to address unmet medical needs. γδ T cells are a specialized population of T cells that possess unique properties, including the ability to differentiate between healthy and diseased tissue. The Company’s pipeline is anchored by INB-600, a novel γδ T cell engager platform with potential applications across oncology and autoimmune indications. IN8bio is also advancing INB-100, an allogeneic γδ T cell candidate for adult patients with high-risk leukemias undergoing haploidentical stem cell transplantation, and INB-200/400, an autologous genetically modified γδ T cell candidate for newly diagnosed glioblastoma (GBM). For more information about IN8bio, visit www.IN8bio.com . (UFG) (Nasdaq: UFCS) today reported financial results for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, with net income increasing 45% over the prior year to $33.4 million ($1.29 per diluted share) and adjusted operating income increasing 42% over the prior year to $33.7 million ($1.30 per diluted share). Net written premium increased 9% in the second quarter, led by growth in the company's core commercial business. The second quarter combined ratio improved 1.1 points year-over-year to 95.3% primarily due to a decreased catastrophe loss ratio. Prior year reserve development remained neutral overall, and net investment income increased 33% to $28.9 million. “UFG delivered another quarter of outstanding results, achieving our best second-quarter combined ratio in more than 15 years, record net income, record net written premium, and the highest investment income in over 10 years,” said President and CEO Kevin Leidwinger. “These results contributed to a 13.2% return on equity through the first six months of 2026, marking our strongest year-to-date financial performance in two decades. “The momentum we are seeing reflects the benefits of the strategic actions we have taken to deepen underwriting expertise, evolve our capabilities, strengthen alignment with our distribution partners, and improve investment returns. The transformation of our business continues to generate meaningful financial and operational results, positioning UFG for long-term success. “As we enter the second half of the year, we remain focused on leveraging our underwriting expertise and strong distribution relationships to pursue attractive growth opportunities. title: Cosmic Rundown: Mario Meets Pareto, AI Agents Miss Threats, and Meta Ships Muse Code
summary: Daily developer news: Pareto optimization explained via Mario. Humans miss 33% of AI agent threats. Meta ships Muse Code. Zed DeltaDB. Branchless Rust 4x speedup.
body_text: Mario meets the Pareto frontier Dominik Mayer published an interactive exploration of Pareto optimization using Super Mario Bros speedruns as the teaching example. The piece walks through how optimizing for multiple objectives simultaneously (completion time, coin collection, enemy defeats) creates trade-off curves where improving one metric necessarily sacrifices another. The Hacker News discussion expanded into applications beyond gaming: API design choices, infrastructure cost versus latency, and the decisions content teams make when balancing SEO against readability. The Wikipedia article on Pareto fronts also hit the front page as readers went deeper. For anyone building systems that serve multiple stakeholders, this framing helps explain why there is rarely a single "best" solution. A headless CMS optimizes across developer experience, editor usability, API performance, and cost. Understanding where your project sits on these trade-off curves clarifies which compromises you are actually making. Humans miss one in three AI agent threats A study across 40,000 game runs found that humans approved 33% of malicious commands when acting as the approval layer for AI agents. The research tested scenarios where an AI agent requested permissions that would enable harmful actions, and human operators routinely clicked through without reading. The discussion raised uncomfortable questions about the "human in the loop" assumption that underlies most AI safety frameworks. If humans rubber-stamp agent requests at this rate in a controlled study, production systems face real exposure. This connects directly to how teams deploy AI agents for content operations. Cosmic's AI agents include approval gates and activity logs specifically because autonomous systems need oversight that actually works. The alternative is hoping your team reads every prompt before approving it, and the data suggests that hope is misplaced. Meta ships Muse Code and Muse Spark 1.2 Meta released Muse Code and updated Muse Spark to 1.2 , expanding their open model offerings. Muse Code targets programming tasks while Spark 1.2 improves on the general-purpose reasoning model. The thread compared these releases against Claude, GPT-4, and other frontier models. Several commenters noted that Meta's open weights approach creates different deployment options than API-only providers, particularly for teams with privacy requirements or cost constraints at scale. For content infrastructure, more capable open models mean more options for self-hosted generation pipelines. A CMS with a REST API can integrate with whichever model fits the use case rather than being locked to a single provider. Zed announces DeltaDB Zed DeltaDB introduces a new approach to collaborative editing state. Rather than traditional operational transforms or CRDTs, DeltaDB uses a delta-based synchronization model that the Zed team claims offers better performance characteristics for their editor. The discussion got technical quickly, with debate about the trade-offs compared to established approaches. For teams building collaborative features, the architectural decisions here are worth studying regardless of whether you use Zed. Branchless Rust: 4x faster filters Sergey Potapov wrote about making a Rust filter 4x faster by removing an if statement . The technique eliminates branch misprediction penalties by computing both paths and selecting the result with arithmetic instead of branching. This kind of optimization matters when processing large datasets, including the content queries that power modern websites. A headless CMS API that filters and transforms content on every request benefits from exactly these kinds of performance improvements in the underlying infrastructure. Quick hits ProvenMetal (YC S26) launched on Hacker News with a pitch to deliver circuit boards in days instead of weeks. Hardware iteration speed directly affects how quickly IoT and embedded teams can ship. The Channels SDK lets developers bring AI agents to Slack, Teams, and other platforms . Multi-channel deployment is becoming table stakes for agent frameworks. Nashville blocked a data center near its zoo using eminent domain . Infrastructure siting fights are intensifying as compute demand grows. GitHub Actions experienced degraded availability , per the status page . CI/CD outages are a reminder that deployment pipelines need resilience planning. Someone built a Nintendo 64 game in 2026 , documented in a detailed making-of post . Retro hardware constraints force creative problem-solving that modern abundance sometimes obscures. Building content infrastructure that keeps pace with these developments means choosing tools designed for flexibility. Cosmic's AI agents handle content generation with proper oversight. The REST API integrates with any model or framework. Start building for free and see how modern content infrastructure supports the workflows these tools enable.

title: When Growth Outpaces the Spreadsheet
summary: Every developer starts small. A handful of sites, a founding team who knows every project by name, and a shared spreadsheet that gets updated whenever someone remembers to do it. At 50 sites, this works fine. The person managing the portfolio can hold most of it in their head, and the spreadsheet is more of […]
body_text: Every developer starts small. A handful of sites, a founding team who knows every project by name, and a shared spreadsheet that gets updated whenever someone remembers to do it. At 50 sites, this works fine. The person managing the portfolio can hold most of it in their head, and the spreadsheet is more of a shared notepad than a system of record. The problem is that growth doesn’t ask permission. And what works cleanly at 50 sites starts to break down long before you reach 500. At 50 sites: manageable, if fragile With a portfolio this size, a small team can usually track site status, interconnection progress, and construction milestones through a mix of memory, email threads, and a spreadsheet that gets updated after the fact. It’s not elegant, but it’s survivable. If someone asks “where do things stand with Project 23,” there’s a good chance someone on the team just knows. The fragility is easy to miss at this stage because it hasn’t caused a visible failure yet. The information exists, just not in a form that scales. It lives in one or two people’s heads, in scattered email threads, and in a spreadsheet that’s only as current as the last time someone remembered to open it. Somewhere between 250 and 500 sites: the wheels start to wobble This is where most developers we talk to say the cracks start to show. The team has grown, but not proportionally to the complexity of the portfolio. More projects are moving through site acquisition, interconnection, and construction simultaneously, and no single person can hold the full picture anymore. The spreadsheet is now being updated by multiple people, on different cadences, with different levels of diligence. Version conflicts creep in. Someone updates a site’s status locally but forgets to push it to the shared file. A project manager assumes a milestone happened because it’s marked complete, when actually the mark was made three weeks before the milestone was even confirmed. Meanwhile, the questions leadership asks get harder to answer quickly. “Which projects are behind on interconnection?” used to be something you could answer from memory. Now it requires someone spending an afternoon reconciling five different sources before they can say anything with confidence. At 500+ sites: the old approach doesn’t just wobble, it fails Past a certain point, the manual approach doesn’t just become inefficient. It becomes actively unreliable. The gap between what’s happening in the field and what’s reflected in your tracking system grows wide enough that decisions get made on outdated information. A capacity offer gets missed because nobody flagged the deadline in time. A construction crew shows up to a site missing a lease detail that was known internally but never made it into the file they were working from. This is also the point where the cost of the old approach becomes visible in ways leadership can’t ignore. Not because someone finally built a better spreadsheet, but because the fundamental model, information scattered across people and files, stops being able to support a portfolio at this scale, no matter how disciplined the team is about updating it. Why this isn’t a discipline problem It’s tempting to treat this as a process failure: if the team were just better about updating the spreadsheet, this wouldn’t happen. But that framing misses what’s actually going on. No amount of individual diligence fixes a structural problem. A spreadsheet, however well maintained, is a single static snapshot updated by hand. It was never built to reflect the real-time state of a growing, multi-stage portfolio, and no team discipline changes that fact. The fix isn’t better habits. It’s a system where site, project, and asset data live in one place that updates as work happens, not one that depends on someone remembering to type it in afterward. What to watch for in your own portfolio If your team is somewhere in that 250 to 500 range, or approaching it, a few signs tend to show up before the fully unmanageable stage does: leadership questions that used to get answered in a sentence now take an afternoon of reconciliation. Different people on the team have different answers to the same status question. And someone, usually without saying it out loud, has started keeping their own shadow tracker because they don’t fully trust the shared one anymore. None of these are signs of a bad team. They’re signs of a system that was built for a smaller version of the business than the one you’re now running. It’s worth addressing before the gap between what’s tracked and what’s actually happening gets wide enough to cost you a project. title: Better Ideas Begin with Better Understanding
summary: One of the things I enjoy most about working at our company is collaborating with people from around the world. On our Sustainability team, projects regularly involve employees across multiple countries and cultures. Every conversation is a chance to learn something new, not just about the work itself, but about how people communicate and solve problems.
body_text: By Carolina Palma, Risk & Sustainability Analyst One of the things I enjoy most about working at our company is collaborating with people from around the world. On our Sustainability team, projects regularly involve employees across multiple countries and cultures. Every conversation is a chance to learn something new, not just about the work itself, but about how people communicate and solve problems. This led me to complete the Culture Map assessment. I wanted to better understand how people from different cultures prefer to communicate so I could work more effectively with teams across our global organization. One lesson stood out immediately: Communication is about much more than language. Different cultures have different expectations around feedback, relationship building, responsiveness and even everyday interactions. Something as simple as how you greet someone or how much context you include in an email can shape how they receive your message. Rather than expecting everyone to communicate the same way, I’ve learned to pay closer attention to the people I’m working with. I adapt my communication based on what helps them feel comfortable and understood. That adaptability builds trust. Trust grows when people know you’ll deliver what you’ve committed to and communicate openly. Those habits matter regardless of where someone lives, but understanding cultural differences makes it easier to build those relationships. I’ve experienced that firsthand with my own team. Although we’re located in Spain, the United States and the Czech Republic, we’ve built strong connections by communicating regularly and sharing our work openly, making time for one another through weekly meetings and individual conversations. Even though we’re fully remote, we’ve created a team environment where everyone feels included and supported. The Culture Map also reminded me that no one fits perfectly into a national stereotype. When I reviewed my results, I realized my own communication style didn’t fully align with what someone might typically expect from someone in Spain. It reflected experiences I’ve gained from working internationally and reinforced that every person brings their own perspective to the table. That’s one of the greatest strengths of a global company. When people from different backgrounds collaborate , we challenge assumptions, share new ideas and develop better solutions than any one perspective could create alone. The more we understand one another, the stronger we become together.

What to Tell Your Convention Photographer Before the Doors Open
summary: How to brief a convention photographer so three days on the show floor turns into a year of marketing assets, not 4,000 unusable frames.
body_text: The most expensive three days of your marketing year Your VP's twenty minutes on stage. This frame is how the other eleven months see it. Your best engineer had a twenty-minute conversation with a prospect that closes next quarter. Then someone took 4,000 photos on a rented DSLR, dumped them in a shared drive, and nobody opened the folder again. That is the real failure mode of convention photography. Not bad lighting or missed moments. The images exist and never get used, while the event that produced them was the densest gathering of your customers, prospects, and employees all year. Freeman's trends research, drawn from a survey of more than 4,700 attendees and 185 event organizers, found 70% of attendees rank in-person events as their primary learning channel, above every digital option. Bizzabo's data shows 78% of organizers call in-person conferences their most impactful marketing channel, and the CEIR Total Index is forecast to grow 2.1% in 2026. Companies are spending more on the floor. Most still treat what happens on it as a memory rather than an asset. What a convention photographer should actually be briefed to shoot Wide for the recap, tight for LinkedIn, one vertical crop. Brief all three up front. The default brief is "get good photos of the booth." That produces a folder of wide shots with nobody in them, taken during the dead hour before doors opened. A useful brief works backward from where the images will live. Four buckets cover most of it. Booth activity with real people in frame. Not the empty build. Demos in progress, a rep mid-explanation, hands on a product, the crowd two-deep at 11am. Nielsen Norman Group's eyetracking research is blunt on why: users ignore stock photos of generic people and pay sustained attention to information-carrying images. Your booth photos compete against stock, so they should not look like it. Session and stage coverage. A photographer with a lit corner of the booth can shoot twenty consistent portraits in ninety minutes, and those run on the website, in decks, and in every bylined article for two years. Attendee and hallway moments. These are what make a recruiting page or next year's promo look like somewhere people want to be. As we cover in our guide to taking better event photographs , unposed frames almost always outperform arranged ones. The shot list is the deliverable, not the photos Nobody shoots a usable panel frame by accident. It gets briefed or it gets missed. The gap between a good convention shoot and a wasted one is almost never the photographer's skill. It is that nobody told them which twelve images marketing needed by Monday. Before the show, write down the placements: recap blog header, three LinkedIn carousel frames, the sales deck slide, the careers page refresh, next year's event landing page. Work back to the shots that fill them, hand the photographer the list on paper, and name one person reachable on the floor. This is where returns compound. Bizzabo found 82% of organizers create video-on-demand content from their events, and the same logic applies to stills. Content Marketing Institute's survey of 1,015 B2B marketers found 33% planning to increase experiential investment in 2026, and among those measuring results, 51% reported shorter sales cycles. Imagery is what carries that spend into the other eleven months. Our piece on how top event managers get the best photos goes deeper on shoot day. Booking coverage across a multi-city show calendar One convention is a logistics problem. A dozen a year across different cities is an operations problem, and it is where in-house approaches break. A vetted photographer in Las Vegas, then Chicago, then Orlando means a new search, a new rate negotiation, and results that look nothing like the last city's. This is the problem Snappr's business events coverage is built for. Shoots book in minutes rather than through a per-city search, guidelines are centralized so every event gallery looks consistent, and edited photos and video come back within days rather than weeks, which is still inside the window where an event recap has reach. Snappr powers visual content for 73% of the Fortune 500 , so the multi-city calendar problem is a familiar one. ‍ Booking event coverage should not feel like project management. Snappr Pro drops the service fee to 9% a shoot and keeps your guidelines and preferred photographers on file, which is most of the consistency problem solved. For a full multi-market program, book time with Snappr's enterprise team to map out your 2026 calendar. Frequently asked questions What does a convention photographer do? A convention photographer covers a multi-day trade show or conference, shooting booth activity, speaker sessions, attendee interactions, and often on-site headshots. The work is briefed around specific marketing placements rather than general documentation, and delivery speed matters because event content loses reach fast. How much does a convention photographer cost? Rates vary by city, duration, and whether editing and rush delivery are included. Multi-day coverage is usually priced per day or half day, with on-site headshot sessions quoted separately. Booking through a platform with fixed rates removes the per-city negotiation on a multi-show calendar. How many photographers do I need for a convention? One covers a single booth and a few sessions comfortably. If you have concurrent speaking slots, a large activation, and a headshot station running at once, you need two. Decide by how many things happen simultaneously, not by the size of the show. How far in advance should I book convention photography? Two to four weeks is comfortable for major shows, since photographers in convention cities book out during peak weeks. Booking through a network rather than a single local shooter gives you more room for late additions and schedule changes. What should I give the photographer before the show? A written shot list tied to specific placements, your booth number and floor plan, the session schedule with speaker names, a named on-site contact, and any brand guidelines. The shot list matters most. It is the difference between 4,000 frames and the twelve images you will actually publish. Sources 1. Today, we continue that mission Doing the right things, the right way. Built by hand. Made in America. And trusted since 1976 . We build homes. title: Wyndham Rewards Ranked #1 by USA TODAY Readers for Ninth Consecutive Year
summary: Latest accolade builds on last month's #1 ranking by US News & World Report; Wyndham Rewards Earner® Card named #1 Travel & Hotel…...
body_text: Latest accolade builds on last month's #1 ranking by US News & World Report; Wyndham Rewards Earner® Card named #1 Travel & Hotel Credit Card for eighth consecutive year HIGHLIGHTS USA TODAY readers voted Wyndham Rewards the No. 1 Hotel Loyalty Program for the ninth consecutive year, building on last month's No. 1 ranking from US News & World Report. Wyndham Rewards Earner® Card named the No. 1 Travel & Hotel Credit Card for the eighth consecutive year, following recent reimagining of co-branded credit card portfolio. The dual No. 1 rankings are a powerful endorsement of Wyndham Rewards' uncomplicated, high-value approach to loyalty, prioritizing simple fixed redemptions and generous rewards. PARSIPPANY, N.J. , Aug 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Wyndham Rewards®, the loyalty program of Wyndham Hotels & Resorts with more than 126 million enrolled members worldwide, has once again been voted the No. 1 Hotel Loyalty Program in the USA TODAY 10Best Readers' Choice Awards , marking its ninth consecutive year atop the rankings. Readers also named the Wyndham Rewards Earner® Card the No. 1 Hotel Credit Card for the eighth consecutive year. The rankings reflect what members value most: a loyalty program that continues to be among the most rewarding in the industry, offering simple, fixed redemptions with no dynamic pricing—meaning no increased points requirements based on seasonality or peak periods of demand. They also mark the latest in a growing list of accolades for Wyndham Rewards, which just last month was also named the #1 hotel rewards program by U.S. News & World Report . Those rankings rate programs based on ease of earning a free night, member benefits, geographic footprint and hotel quality, among other categories. "Great loyalty programs don't just reward travel—they give members a reason to keep coming back. Our focus has always been on delivering meaningful value, whether a member is checking a bucket-list destination off their list or simply making everyday spending more rewarding. Seeing travelers continue to rank the program #1 is a powerful validation that we're delivering on what our members expect. It's recognition we're incredibly proud of, and a credit to the teams, franchisees and strategic partners who make it possible every day." - Scott Strickland, Chief Commercial Officer, Wyndham Hotels & Resorts Designed for the Everyday Travele r Spanning thousands of hotels, vacation club resorts and vacation rentals across 100 countries—from everyday roadside stays to upscale, luxury and all-inclusive resorts—Wyndham Rewards stands apart from other hotel loyalty programs by keeping rewards refreshingly simple. Members earn a minimum of 1,000 points with every qualified stay, and free night redemption tiers start at just 7,500 points per night—soon to drop to 5,000 points next month—making it easy to know what it takes to earn a free night. And those points can take members far beyond a free night. Members can also use them to bid on once-in-a-lifetime experiences through Wyndham Rewards Experiences , from live events and sporting experiences with partners like Madison Square Garden and Caesars Rewards, to entire vacations booked in one place with Wyndham Travel Bundles , making it easy to earn and redeem points across hotels, flights, cruises, rental cars and activities. And with Wyndham Rewards Insider , the program's first-ever travel subscription, members can unlock even more—including automatic Gold level status, travel savings across hotels, flights, cruises, car rentals and more, plus enhanced points-earning opportunities, all designed to make every trip go further. A Credit Card Portfolio Built to Match Wyndham Rewards gets even better with its lineup of co-branded credit cards, issued in partnership with Barclays: the Wyndham Rewards Earner® Card, Earner® Plus Card, Earner® Business Card and the new Earner® Premier Card—Wyndham's first premium credit card. Reimagined earlier this year, the refreshed portfolio expands everyday earnings, booking benefits and cardmember value across the lineup. Cardmembers earn accelerated points on stays at Hotels by Wyndham and on everyday purchases like dining, grocery, gas and EV charging, while every card carries elevated Wyndham Rewards status, discounted free night redemptions, while select cards also include Points Payback, which turns points into statement credits toward any purchase. The Earner® Card remains the portfolio's anchor, built for everyday travelers who want real value without an annual fee. At the top of the lineup, the new Earner® Premier Card delivers the richest benefits in the portfolio, offering a 25% discount on free night redemptions, more than $400 in annual value, including complimentary Wyndham Rewards Insider membership and, for the first time in the portfolio, points that never expire. To learn more about Wyndham Rewards or to join for free, visit WyndhamRewards.com . For more on the Wyndham Rewards Earner® credit card suite, or to apply, visit WyndhamRewardsCreditCard.com . USA TODAY 10Best Readers' Choice nominees are curated by a panel of travel industry experts, with winners selected by popular vote. U.S. News & World Report evaluated 13 hotel loyalty programs on membership benefits, network coverage, ease of earning and redeeming points, property diversity and hotel quality. About Wyndham Rewards Part of Wyndham Hotels & Resorts (NYSE: WH), Wyndham Rewards is the #1 hotel rewards, recognized by both U.S. News & World Report and readers of USA TODAY. With more than 126 million enrolled members worldwide, members earn a guaranteed 1,000 points with every qualified stay and can redeem for free nights at thousands of hotels, vacation club resorts and vacation rentals globally starting at just 7,500 points. In addition, through Wyndham Rewards Experiences , members can use points to bid on unforgettable experiences and live events while Wyndham Rewards Insider —a first of its kind travel subscription—offers exclusive savings and perks beyond just hotels, including on flights, cruises, car rentals and more. Join Wyndham Rewards for free at WyndhamRewards.com . You can also like and follow us on Facebook , Instagram and TikTok .
